title: Initiate and maintain first line discipline

lessons.title: Discipline as a supervisor's tool
lessons.html:
What first line discipline means

As a dairy supervisor you are the first line of management. You see the work every day, so you are the first person to notice when a worker breaks a rule or does not perform. First line discipline means dealing with these problems early, fairly and consistently, before they grow into serious cases.

The aim of discipline is to correct behaviour, not to punish. A good milker who arrives late three times needs a conversation and a clear expectation, not a dismissal.

The legal framework

  • The Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 protects workers against unfair dismissal and unfair labour practices.
  • Schedule 8 of the LRA, the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, sets out how discipline should be handled: rules must be known, discipline should be progressive and corrective, and workers must be given a fair hearing.
  • The Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 sets working hours, leave and other conditions that also apply on farms.
  • Disputes can be referred to the CCMA.

The farm's disciplinary code

Every farm should have a written disciplinary code and procedure. It lists rules and the likely sanction for each offence. Typical dairy farm rules include:

  • Arriving on time for milking, which cannot wait.
  • Following the milking routine and keeping treated milk out of the tank.
  • No alcohol or drugs at work.
  • Treating animals humanely, as the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 requires.
  • Following safety rules and wearing protective equipment.

As supervisor you must know the code, explain it to your team and make sure new workers receive it in a language they understand. A worker cannot fairly be disciplined for breaking a rule they did not know about, unless the rule is obvious, such as not stealing.

Consistency

Treat similar offences in the same way for all workers. If you ignore one person's late coming and discipline another, the process becomes unfair and the team loses trust in you.

lessons.title: Handling minor misconduct and warnings
lessons.html:
Progressive discipline

Progressive discipline means the response grows stronger if the behaviour continues. A common sequence is:

StepWho usually handles it
Informal counselling or verbal discussionSupervisor
Verbal warning (recorded)Supervisor
Written warningSupervisor or manager
Final written warningManager after an enquiry
DismissalManager after a formal hearing

Serious misconduct, such as theft, assault, gross cruelty to animals or being drunk while driving a tractor, may go straight to a formal hearing. Check your farm's code and your level of authority.

How to hold a corrective discussion

  1. Act soon. Deal with the issue the same day or the next day.
  2. Get the facts. What happened, when, who saw it? Check records such as the clock card or milking times.
  3. Meet in private. Never reprimand a worker in front of the team.
  4. Explain the rule and what the worker did. Stick to facts, not personal opinions.
  5. Listen. Give the worker a chance to explain. There may be a reason, such as a sick child or a transport problem.
  6. Agree on the way forward: what must change and by when.
  7. Record the discussion and outcome, and ask the worker to sign. If they refuse, note this with a witness.

Issuing a warning

A written warning should state the offence, date, the rule broken, the expected improvement, how long the warning stays valid according to the code, and the consequence of repeating the offence. Give the worker a copy. Workers may have a representative, such as a fellow worker or shop steward, as the code allows.

Do not threaten, swear or make promises you cannot keep. Keep your tone calm and respectful.

lessons.title: Poor performance, hearings and records
lessons.html:
Misconduct versus poor performance

Not every problem is misconduct. A worker who will not follow the routine is a misconduct issue. A worker who cannot do it properly, for example a new milker who misses mastitis cases, is a performance issue. Poor performance is handled with training, coaching and support first, giving the worker reasonable time to improve.

Steps for poor performance

  • Set clear standards, for example cows per hour, milking routine steps, records filled in.
  • Show the worker the gap between the standard and their work.
  • Arrange training or coaching and check progress.
  • Record each review. If there is still no improvement after fair support, refer to the manager.

Preparing for a formal hearing

When a case is serious, your role is usually to bring the facts to the manager or chairperson. Prepare:

  1. A short written statement of what happened.
  2. Evidence: records, photos, witness names, previous warnings.
  3. The rule from the disciplinary code that was broken.

The worker must get written notice of the hearing and the charge, enough time to prepare, the right to a representative and an interpreter if needed, and the chance to state their case. The chairperson should be someone who was not involved in the incident.

Keeping records

Keep disciplinary records confidential and filed safely. Good records protect both the worker and the farm if a case goes to the CCMA. Remove expired warnings from active use according to the code.

Preventing problems

Many discipline issues come from unclear instructions, poor housing or transport, or tiredness from long shifts. Talk to your team, fix what you can and raise the rest with management.

Key points

  • Discipline should be corrective, consistent and fair.
  • Know the farm's disciplinary code and the LRA Code of Good Practice: Dismissal.
  • Deal with problems early, in private, and listen to the worker.
  • Handle poor performance with training and support before sanctions.
  • Record every discussion and warning, and keep records confidential.

quiz.question: What is the main aim of first line discipline?

options.text: To reduce the number of workers

quiz.question: Where should a corrective discussion take place?

options.text: In front of the whole team

quiz.question: Which document sets out guidelines for fair dismissal in South Africa?

options.text: Schedule 8 of the Labour Relations Act, the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal

quiz.question: A new milker cannot spot mastitis cases yet. This is best treated as:

options.text: A performance issue needing training and support

quiz.question: Who should chair a formal disciplinary hearing?

options.text: The supervisor who saw the incident
Someone who was not involved in the incident
